en: Shi Dunlun’s Collected Explanations of the Treatise, Fascicle 57.
Thus far, within the extensive analysis of the six types of skillfulness (*kauśalya*), four have already been explained. Hereafter begins the fifth.
The skill in discerning what is possible and what is impossible consists of four parts within this text;
first, the conclusion of the preceding section and the introduction of the subsequent one.
Second, the enumeration of the four gates;
third, the detailed explanation according to those gates;
fourth, the indication of other [topics] not appearing here.
Among the four gates listed,
first, as for "entity":
it is the wisdom that realizes the causal relationship— whether concordant or discordant— of the objects of knowledge.
The essence of skillfulness regarding what is possible and what is impossible (sthānāsthāna-kauśalya).
Second, the manifestation of discernment refers to the causal conditions for the arising of the teaching.
In order to demonstrate that the wisdom of correct skillful means regarding the objects of defilement and purification is free from impairment,
the expertise in what is possible and what is impossible (sthānāsthāna-kauśalya) is taught;
these two belong to the first [category].
Therefore, it is said that "the essence" is the first [topic],
"the manifestation" is the second, "the gates" are the third,
and "the distinctions" are the fourth.
These two belong to the latter [section].
Therefore, it says: "after the differentiation of the gates.
This is explained by way of the gates of reliance (*āśraya*).
This constitutes four sections.
The first two are easily understood.
Regarding the third, the section on the "Explanatory Gates," there are three parts.
First, the meaning is analyzed according to the four gates of establishment and so forth;
next, the meaning is analyzed according to the four principles;
third, the conclusion is joined.
In the first part, four gates are initially opened;
in the latter part, they are analyzed according to those gates.
Within this, the initial section consists of questions and answers that provide a general exposition on the intent of the four gates.

"Because he wishes to manifest the gateways of differentiation in all their various modes" means that he wishes to reveal the meaning of the gateways of differentiation regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*) throughout all phenomena.
Now, the meaning of this third section is explained;
the four sections will subsequently be interpreted in order.
Regarding the first section, it is said:
This refers to the remaining distinct characteristics not subsumed under that [first] gate of accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Jing says:
"It means that based on the first gate of accomplishment, those meanings not subsumed by the other three gates are explained as the 'remaining distinctions' of accomplishment."
I shall now explain this.
For instance, the faculty of the eye cannot accomplish such functions as hearing sounds or smelling odors; therefore, it is said that those [functions] are not subsumed by it.
This is the reverse of its activity.
Regarding what I shall now explain concerning the remaining instances of seeing visible forms apart from those already mentioned:
the visual faculty (cakṣur-indriya) is able to see and accomplish its own function;
it cannot hear sounds, smell odors, or perform other such external functions.
Therefore, it is called the "distinctive characteristic of the remainder. Ji says:
"This refers exclusively to those things established by the initial [classification] that are not subsumed within the aforementioned categories."
This now demonstrates that all various categories are fully subsumed;
these are precisely the final three gates.
As for the term "no place" (asthāna):
Regarding the locations of the ten directions or the three realms,
"without position" refers to the positions of the three periods of time.
Question: The sutras state that those who have attained the stage of mastery can employ the five faculties interchangeably.
Why, then, is it said here that it is impossible for the eye to possess the functions of the other four faculties?
Some say that herein, the possible and the impossible are distinguished with respect to the five faculties in their state of non-mastery.
Question:
If that is so, when mastery has been attained, the four great elements are able to function as one another.
Answer:
According to Master Guo’s interpretation, even in the state of mastery (*vaśitā*), the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are mutually interchangeable.

Therefore, we know that when the Master of the Treatise speaks of the mutual interchangeability of the Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), this statement is also made with reference to the state prior to mastery.
Master Xing of Silla said:
"The four great elements serve as the basis for form;
form itself is not luminous or sharp."
Therefore, even when one has attained the state of supreme mastery, the five sense faculties do not interchange their functions;
the five faculties serve as the basis for the mind,
and the mind is consequently clear and sharp.
If, in a state of mastery, the five sense organs can function through the power of that which they support,
they may also be employed interchangeably;
now, let us examine various explanations on this point.
The *Jishi shuyao* states:
Regarding this mutual functioning of the faculties, there are two differing interpretations.
The first master says:
In reality, they are able to perceive all objects.
The second master explains that within each individual sense organ, all [other] organs are fully present.
Each arises according to its specific function;
it is not that a single faculty perceives all objects.
Because the functions of the various faculties each pervade all [objects], they are called "mutually functioning."
Otherwise, it would follow that they possess the characteristic of being perishable dharmas.
Furthermore, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) would also have to possess a separate function for its own use, and so forth.
According to the second explanation, although one has attained the stage of mastery (*vaśitā*), the eye does not possess the functions of the four faculties.
The earth element also does not perform the functions of the other three great elements;
this accords well with the text,
and thus there is no contradiction.
Second is the section on the gate of conjunction and assembly, which has six successive expositions.
Regarding the second [exposition], it says: "The coarse divisions of water and fire."
This briefly refers to the subtle fire of the sensation of heat within water;
for instance, because the coarse fire of charcoal does not coexist with water.
As for the fourth and fifth [points]:
There is no place or occasion where two mind-kings, two feelings, two mental factors, and so forth, of the same category as a single visual consciousness, could coincide and assemble simultaneously.
Furthermore, there is no instance where a single visual consciousness could simultaneously be associated with both the wholesome and the unwholesome, or with both suffering and pleasure.
Third is the section on the gate of realization,
which contains seven successive expositions;
these specifically focus on the fourth, fifth, and seventh [expositions] to establish the names by which they are realized.
Regarding those born as *paṇḍaka* (eunuchs),
they are so by birth;
in reality, all five types of *paṇḍaka* are incapable of producing either male or female offspring.
However, according to the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*, it refers exclusively to the "born hermaphrodite" (*jāti-paṇḍaka*).
Next, regarding the section on the manifestation of activity (*samudācāra-mukha*), there are seven successive expositions.
These all analyze what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*) within the context of phenomena currently arising; thus, they are termed the "section on the manifestation of activity."
Regarding the statement that it is impossible for one who does not sever craving and so forth to attain [the supramundane],
this means that during the stage of being with outflows (sāsrava), one must first subdue craving before giving rise to the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-saṃjñā) and other such practices;
furthermore, it is through the accomplishment of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) that the cultivation of the outflow-free (anāsrava) occurs.
Next, the possible and the impossible are distinguished according to the four principles,
as in the text.
Fourth is the section on the gate of differentiation.
The skill in discerning what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*) is distinguished from the skill in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*);
because the meanings and implications of these two skills overlap,
they are contrasted here.
The others are not so. The domain of skillfulness regarding what is possible and what is impossible (sthānāsthāna-kauśalya) is broad,
whereas that of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) is narrow.
In the sixth section below, which distinguishes skill in the faculties (*indriya-kauśalya*),
first there is the summary of what precedes and the introduction of what follows;
subsequently, the chapters are opened for explanation.
Within this, the first half-verse enumerates four gates. As for their meaning:
first, the definition of the sense-faculties (*indriya*).
"Intention" refers to the meaning of the second [section], the exposition of the faculties (*indriya*).
"Establishment" refers to the third [section], the formal establishment and rejection of the faculties.
"Extensive analysis for what follows" refers to the fourth [section], the detailed discrimination of their sequence.
Second, the explanation according to the gateway [of meaning] consists of four sections.
First, regarding the explanation that the meaning of "superiority" (*adhipati*) is the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*):
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* also states: "Although all conditioned phenomena possess predominance (*adhipatya*),
it is only those that are preeminent that are established as faculties (*indriya*),
just as in the cases of a sovereign or a lord of gods."
Regarding the meaning of the second explanation:
in order to manifest the most preeminent significance of various matters and various phenomena,
one shall now explain the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching on the faculties (*indriya*).
As stated in the *Vibhāṣā*:
There was a brahmin named Janman who had previously studied the meaning of the faculties (*indriya*).
Having heard various divergent explanations regarding the establishment of the faculties (indriya), many were unable to understand them.
They went to where the Buddha was and asked,
"Gautama, there are many who speak of the faculties."
"How many faculties (*indriya*) do you now definitively establish?
The Buddha said,
"As for the designation 'birth,' although I possess wisdom, I cannot add one or subtract one from among the twenty-two faculties."
Now, in order to explain the Buddha’s sūtras, I have made this statement.
To manifest the most excellent meaning regarding various matters and various phenomena,
I have taught these twenty-two faculties (*indriya*).
In the third section, which distinguishes the establishment and rejection [of the faculties],
the first eight successive expositions correctly establish the faculties,
while the final verse summarizes these eight gates.
First, the faculties (indriya) are established based on six meanings.
As the verse in the Abhidharmakośa says:
"The mind and its mental concomitants depend upon these for their differentiation."
This is abiding; this is affliction;
this is the equipment; this is purification.
It is by virtue of these measures that the faculties are established.
Regarding the basis of the mental factors (*caitta*):
the six faculties, such as the eye, are established as the bases for the six consciousnesses.
This is their distinction.
This is the second [point] establishing the two faculties of male and female.
By means of these two faculties, there is differentiation among sentient beings as well as differentiation in their characteristics.
This refers to abiding.
This third condition establishes the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*),
because it enables one to remain for the duration of a single lifetime.
This refers to the defiled state.
The five faculties of sensation (*pañca-vedanendriya*) are established;
this refers to the predominance of the experience of the fruits of karma.
That anxiety is not the fruit;
however, once the fruit has been attained,
one still gives rise to its enjoyment within the state of that fruition.
This refers to the fruit of enjoyment.
These provisions consist of establishing the five faculties, such as faith and the rest.
Because these are the provisions for the noble path,
this purity establishes the characteristics of the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya).
This treatise is also similar in meaning to that [text].
Among the second five meanings,
the two faculties of male and female receive the hidden object of sexual intercourse.
Therefore, it is called the predominance of the enjoyment of hidden objects.
Regarding the third of the five meanings,
the six sense faculties mostly enjoy their own internal selves.
The two faculties of male and female with respect to objects are termed "external doors" because they experience the bodies of others.
The five feeling faculties are capable of experiencing both external objects and the internal body.
Based on the production of afflictions (*saṃkleśa*) and the establishment of their antidotes, eight faculties are established.
Regarding the fourth of the six meanings, "that which causes the basis to function according to its mastery," Jing says:
"Because the sovereign mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) is established within this present body."
Now, consulting the *Abhidharmakośa*, it says:
"That which follows at will" means that as the Sūtra states: "The mind leads the world; the mind thoroughly governs it. Thus, this single dharma—the mind—follows at will.
Regarding dependence on benefit and harm:
joy and pleasure benefit the body,
while sorrow and suffering harm it.
The category of "abandonment" applies to both [the preceding and the following].
Within the fifth and sixth meanings,
the six faculties, such as the eye, are established as the essence of sentient beings.
The six faculties belong to sentient beings.
Regarding the establishment of five faculties as the means for superior rebirth,
Jing says that the five faculties beginning with faith (śraddhā) are common to both the out-flowing (sāsrava) and the non-out-flowing (anāsrava).
Defiled faith and so forth induce superior births among gods and humans;
untainted faith and so forth perfume defiled karma to induce superior births in the five pure abodes.
Therefore, in this current explanation, only the defiled [faith] is taken as that which induces superior births.
The untainted faculties of faith and so forth mutually belong to the three roots;
they are the definitive and superior means for attaining the realization of nirvana.
This is the sixth of the five meanings.
The six faculties, beginning with the eye, are established to manifest the essence of sentient beings.
Similarly, the two faculties of male and female are established to manifest the nourishment and growth of all sentient beings;
the previous explanation was based on birth.
This is based on the increase [of lifespan];
it establishes a single life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) to manifest that the lifespan of sentient beings gradually diminishes.
The former [case] is based on their abiding and passing away during a time of flourishing, when there is joy and pleasure.
During times of decline, there is sorrow and suffering;
equanimity pertains to both times.
The former is based on the enjoyment of sensory objects.
Regarding the establishment of the eight faculties to clarify the meaning of the virtues and faults of sentient beings,
Jing says:
"This is to manifest that faith and the other [faculties] are dharmas of virtue."
Because they can remedy faults,
eight faculties are established.
Ji (Jizang) says:
That is to say, among the three untainted [faculties] and the five beginning with faith, those that constitute the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) are meritorious qualities.
The five beginning with faith are the portion of merit (*puṇyabhāga*).
Those that are tainted (*sāsrava*) are defects.
Furthermore, "virtues" refers to the eight faculties;
"faults" refers to that which is abandoned by the eight faculties.
This occurs within the two categories of the seventh [ground].
It is established by means of eight designative phrases.
Based on such a name, it is called the first, namely,
the essence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Lineage is the second,
meaning the lineage of one's parents, such as the Kāśyapa clan or the Kṣatriya caste.
Thus, experiencing suffering and pleasure is the third.
That is to say, depending on excellent food and drink, one experiences joy and pleasure;
depending on poor food and drink, one experiences sorrow and suffering, and so forth.
Thus, there are four kinds of lifespan.
Thus, abiding constitutes five [categories],
and lifespan constitutes the sixth.
These are established according to the section on householders.
In this way, from faith up to wisdom, one establishes the five faculties beginning with faith as the seventh.
Likewise, for the sake of progressing toward the fruit, one establishes the final three untainted faculties as the eighth designation.
This is based on the category of those who have gone forth.
Regarding the eighth of the six meanings:
since the six faculties, such as the eye, are capable of producing various faults,
one should exercise restraint over these faculties.
Thus, by means of that which is capable of guarding, the six factors to be guarded are established as roots.
It is because of these that men and women are able to go forth and realize the fruits [of the path].
Because there is life, one dwells in the world and accumulates wholesome qualities.
By means of knowing that the five feelings give rise to various defilements, one acts with correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*).
The remainder of the text may be understood accordingly.
Next, there is one verse that concludes the eight successive sections.
"Turning according to objects" and so forth concludes the first section;
"by means of manifestation" concludes the second.
The "inner gate" constitutes the third summary;
the "ornamentation" constitutes the fourth.
Regarding the two types of sentient beings:
the first two constitute the fifth and sixth [fetters],
while the provisional designation constitutes the seventh.
The eighth section on the protection from fetters.
From here below begins the fourth [major] section, the gate of detailed analysis.
This is divided into two parts.
First, there is a brief analysis by means of eight sections;
subsequently, there is a further detailed analysis by means of six sections.
Within the former, the eight sections are first distinguished.
It concludes later with a verse.
Within the preceding section, there are six rounds of question and answer concerning the first gate of activity.
Finally, regarding those who attain nirvana through the three faculties:
To explain this generally according to both distant and near perspectives:
the former two have the function of tending toward nirvāṇa,
while the latter one has the function of directly realizing nirvāṇa.
Second is the gate of the conventional and the real:
the two faculties of male and female are conventionally established upon the body faculty;
the life faculty is established based on the states of the ālayavijñāna.
The three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) take nine faculties as their substance;
therefore, six are nominally existent.
This concludes the third section: the classification of matter and mind.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the analysis of mutual inclusion based on the five dharmas;
second, the clarification of their respective categories by citing the provisional bases.
Among these, the five faculties beginning with the eye, as well as the male and female faculties, are material form (*rūpa*).
The mental faculty (*manas*) and the mental faculty within the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) are mind (*citta*).
The five faculties of faith and so forth, together with the five sensations (*vedanā*), constitute ten in total.
Furthermore, among the three untainted [aggregates], with the exception of mind,
the remainder are mental factors;
the life-faculty is a dissociated formation.
All of these are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and thus knowable.
In the second section of the text,
it is stated that the latter three faculties are states (*avasthā*) of nine faculties.
This refers to the five faculties beginning with faith and the three types of feeling.

For example, as in the ninth chapter of the *Abhidharma*, the faculty of "the faculty of knowing what is not yet known" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) adds the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) to those [five].
In this treatise, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) consisting of fifteen moments of mind is designated as "the faculty of knowing what is not yet known."
Because there is no sorrow (*daurmanasya*) therein, there are nine [faculties].
Since those [beings] take as their initial faculty the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*),
there are ten [faculties] when sorrow is added.
Regarding the statement that "the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) has no [separate] locus," the Tripiṭaka Master says:
"Thus we know that the life-faculty is not established solely upon the eighth mind-king (citta-rāja), but rather extends across the five simultaneous mental factors (caitta)."
Master Ji said:
"The current interpretation is not correct;
it contradicts the text of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*."
Furthermore, both the fundamental [faculties] and their remaining derivative powers—
such as the male, female, and the three untainted faculties—
all take a small portion of the sense organ upon which they rely as their substance.
It resembles the mind of its own original nature;
this is a designation established based upon the former, and is not a portion of the characteristics of the basis itself.
Therefore, it is said to have no specific affiliation.
This does not mean that it is established based upon all five mental factors (*caitasika*) in general.
Master Jing’s commentary states:
"The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is established based on the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*); when it is said to have no specific affiliation, it refers to this."
This category is established as a conventional designation based on the states of resultant matter and mind;
it is not subsumed under any other specific category.
Now, let us consult the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
The life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is conventionally established based solely on seeds and not on actual manifestation; therefore,
it should be understood that this text [refers to] that which is not subsumed under the manifest faculties.
Therefore, it is said that [the life-faculty] has no affiliation.
Furthermore, it is explained that the life-faculty is neither form nor mind.
Therefore, there is nothing to which it belongs.
Fourth is the gate of the three natures, beginning with the wholesome.
First, the nature of the wholesome itself is analyzed according to three meanings.
First, regarding the conventional and the real:
in total, there are eight,
namely the five beginning with faith and the three untainted [faculties].
Second, setting aside the general discussion to speak of the pure [faculties],
which are the five beginning with faith;
third, selecting from the general category by means of specific distinction.
That is to say, it consists of portions of six [factors].

Namely, the mental faculty (*manas*) and the five sensations (*vedanā*), including sorrow (*daurmanasya*), which pertain to both the wholesome and the unwholesome; taking only their wholesome aspects constitutes "portions.
Furthermore, the four sensations and the mental faculty, which pertain to all three natures (wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral); taking only their wholesome aspects constitutes "portions."
Next, the unwholesome [dharmas] are distinguished as being a small portion of six;
this is treated similarly to what was previously discussed regarding the indeterminate, which has two meanings:
first, setting aside the mixed to discuss the pure.
That is to say, the seven [mental factors] and life-force.
Second, by way of general exclusion,
one selects [the factors] excluding the four feelings of grief and the mental faculty.
All [of these] pertain to the three natures;
it is only by taking the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) that they are termed "partial.
The fifth [category] consists of those with maturation (*savipāka*), and so forth.
The seventh section of questions and answers:
First, identifying those with maturation (vipāka).

This refers to the entirety of mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*), as well as four other types of feeling—namely, receiving (*vedanā*) and so forth—and a small portion of the five mental factors (*manopavicāra*).
This is because those that are neutral (*avyākṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) have been excluded.
Second, it is explained that there are no ripened effects (*avipāka*):
namely, the seven material [faculties], the life-faculty, and the three untainted [faculties] in their entirety.
The first eight are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), while the latter three are untainted (*anāsrava*).

This is explained with reference to the initial faculties within the path of vision (*darśanamārga*); it refers to the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) and the four feelings (*vedanā*) together with the mental faculty (*manas*), excluding the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and wholesome-tainted (*kuśala-sāsrava*) factors.
Third, the explanation of the accompanying factors that possess maturation:
the superior retributions of humans and devas cause the physical basis upon which the noble path arises to gradually increase in excellence.
Because these characteristics are mutually dependent,
they perfume the seeds that give rise to the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa),
and through the power of the ultimate concentration of the untainted (anāsrava), they prolong karmic retribution.
Fourth, the discrimination of maturation (*vipāka*).
"A small portion of one" refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) in its entirety.
The seven material [faculties], the mind-faculty (*manas*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) each take a small portion.
Regarding the seven material faculties, they take the retribution-born (*vipākaja*) and exclude the nurtured (*aupacayika*), taking only the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Regarding the mind-faculty and equanimity, they exclude the equanimity associated with the seven consciousnesses; this is termed "a small portion."
As stated in the Abhidharmābhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra:
"The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is indeterminate by nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*);
that which lacks the characteristics of maturation (*vipāka-lakṣaṇa*) is indeterminate as maturation (*vipāka-avyākṛta*)."
The Tripitaka Master says:
"There is no contradiction here;
the Abhidharma (Dharma-lakṣaṇa) analyzes [reality] in terms of the three natures."
The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is inherently indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) among the three natures;
therefore, it is called "indeterminate by nature.
As for its substance, it is exclusively maturation-indeterminate (*vipāka-avyākṛta*).
Furthermore, another interpretation is that the Abhidharma establishes the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneity) based on the aggregates (*skandha*) according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*),
and establishes the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) based on the duration of that homogeneity.
Therefore, those [factors] are not merely indeterminate by nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*) because they are maturation (*vipāka*); rather,
the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is established here among the five aggregates according to the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*),
and it is established as the life-faculty most strongly based on the factors that are maturation.
Therefore, it is said that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is exclusively a result of maturation (*vipāka*).
According to the Sarvāstivāda school, resultant matter (*vipākaja-rūpa*) is established as being without interruption;
however, if one allows for the possibility of interruptions in the resultant mind (*vipākaja-citta*), [the same would apply].
In the Mahāyāna school, there is no such thing as an uninterrupted state of form and mind; rather, these must necessarily be a continuous succession of maturation (*vipāka*).

Therefore, when it is said that "mind abandons" maturation, this refers exclusively to the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and its associated mental factors abandoning [the state of maturation].
Fifth, regarding the statement that all possess seeds of maturation (*vipāka*):
the Tripiṭaka Master says this means they are maintained within the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
"All [phenomena] are called 'maturation' (vipāka).
Furthermore, another interpretation states:
"In this context, those that are based on a continuity (saṃtati) are designated as 'maturation'."
Because all seeds are thus continuous,
they are all termed "maturation" (*vipāka*).
Master Bei Jing said:
Because all seeds that are identical to the ālayavijñāna are termed "maturation" (vipāka),
the twenty-two faculties produced from these maturation-seeds are all termed "born of maturation" (vipākaja).
This passage explains that the untainted seeds (anāsrava-bīja) are termed "maturation" (vipāka) because they share the same basis as their supporting consciousness;
since they have no separate substance,
the three untainted faculties (anāsravendriya) are called "born of maturation" (vipākaja).
Now, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*,
it is said that when the functional capacity of the untainted seeds increases,
this is metaphorically designated as "ripening" (*vipāka*).
Sixth, the discrimination of those that are not maturation (avipāka):
this refers to twelve in their entirety—
namely, the five beginning with faith, the three untainted (anāsrava) faculties, and [the four feelings of] sorrow, joy, pleasure, and pain.
Regarding the nine partial [factors]:
the seven material faculties, the mind faculty, and the equanimity faculty are as previously excluded;
the life-faculty is exclusively maturation (*vipāka*).
Seventh, the explanation of that which arises from maturation (*vipākaja*). All seeds are termed "maturation";
therefore, the various sense faculties (*indriya*) produced from them are called "arisen from maturation."
Within the sixth section, the "Gate of the Distinction of the Three Realms," regarding the four [faculties] of the desire realm:
these are male, female, sorrow, and suffering.
Regarding the "fifteen partials":
this refers to the five faculties, such as the eye, which pertain to both the desire and form realms;
and the life-faculty, which pertains to all three realms.
The five faculties beginning with faith, as well as the mental faculty and the faculty of equanimity, pertain to all three realms as well as to that which is unconditioned (unbound).
The two faculties of joy and pleasure pertain to the desire and form realms as well as to that which is unconditioned.
Since we are now taking only those belonging to the desire realm, it is said that they constitute a portion of fifteen.
Regarding "a portion of fifteen [factors] of the form realm," these are the aforementioned fifteen.
Regarding "a portion of eight [factors] of the formless realm":
That is to say, the five faculties beginning with faith, the mental faculty, the life-faculty, and the equanimity-faculty—
when they are unconditioned (unbound),
they constitute the three untainted faculties in their entirety.
As well as the five faculties beginning with faith;
the portions of joy, pleasure, equanimity, and the mental faculty;
and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) also pertain to the outflow-tainted (sāsrava).
Now, based on those who possess the untainted (*anāsrava*), it is stated generally as "three.
Section seven concerns the gate of the number [of factors] in the various stages (*bhūmi*).
The text is divided into three parts.
First, by way of the stages (bhūmi);
second, by way of being untainted (anāsrava);
third, by way of the degree of maturation.

Regarding the initial statement that "one who has not yet reached the eleventh stage," Jing says this refers to the five faculties beginning with faith, the three untainted [faculties], the mental faculty, joy, and equanimity;
this is a general summary based on the practice of humans in the desire realm.
Question: According to the preceding question and answer, there is also pleasure.
Why is it not mentioned?
Answer:
It is not mentioned because it is provisional. Tai says:
"Excluding the mind, one takes up pleasure."
According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*:
"Question: If the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) possesses joy (*prīti*), why is it not established [as having five factors]? Answer: Because it is unstable.
The intent of this question is as follows: if the first dhyāna possesses joy, it is established as having five factors.
Question: Since there is already the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*) within the stage of the Not-yet-arrived (*anāgamya*), why is it not established as a factor (*aṅga*)?
Answer: The intention [of the response] is as follows.
The stage of "not yet arrived" (anāgamya) possesses joy;
however, because it is still moved by the turbulent winds of the desire realm,
it is not established as having [meditative] factors.
Although you have established its existence,
it is not yet known on what scriptural authority this is based;
therefore, he asks again for what reason this serves as proof.
The answer cites the Buddha’s teaching.
Regarding the statement that the first gate describes the stage of "not-yet-arrived" (*anāgamya*),
this refers to the body being moistened by the joy and bliss born of seclusion.
The section beginning with "pervading" constitutes the subsequent gate, which is the fundamental stage.
This is because at first it only moistens that which is associated with the mind,
whereas subsequently it brings joy throughout the body and other faculties.
The latter is superior while the former is inferior.
Since it is stated that "joy" (*prīti*) implies there is also "bliss" (*sukha*), one might wonder why only the manifest joy is taken here.
This is because the manifest and the implicit mutually inform one another; however, in this instance, only the manifest is selected.
To explain this by means of reasoning:
there is indeed pleasure in this stage as well;
it is called "pleasure" because it gladdens the faculties.
The first and second dhyānas possess eighteen [mental factors],
excluding male-female faculties, grief, and physical suffering.
It was previously stated that bound phenomena (*saṃyojana-dharma*) are exclusively outflows (*āsrava*).
In this context, it is taught that the dharmas based on the stages (bhūmi) encompass both the tainted (sāsrava) and the untainted (anāsrava).
Therefore, the differences between the higher and lower stages do not constitute a fault.
In the third and fourth [dhyānas], joy (prīti) and bliss (sukha) are respectively eliminated in sequence.
Jingyun: Initially, when the first dhyāna has not yet been attained, joy is established as being identical to the root [dhyāna];
the same applies to the second dhyāna.
In the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) of the third dhyāna, joy (*sukha*) is established;
in the preparatory stage of the fourth dhyāna, equanimity (*upekṣā*) is established.
Regarding the eleven [factors] in the lower three formless attainments (*ārūpya*):
This refers to the five faculties beginning with faith, the mental faculty, the life faculty, the equanimity faculty, and the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
Furthermore, regarding the eight [faculties] of the Non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñin*), this is also based on the practice performed by many people.
That is to say, the five faculties beginning with faith, as well as the mental faculty, life, and equanimity.
These are stated solely in terms of their active manifestation (*samudācāra*); if one were to consider them in terms of their seeds (*bīja*), [the count would differ].
Discussing both ordinary beings and sages in general,
all twenty-two faculties can be found present within every stage [of the path].
Jing says:
Question: How can the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) be present in the three formless stages?

As stated in the subsequent text, one enters the path of seeing by relying on the four dhyānas and the initial threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), and relies on nine meditative attainments to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*).

The answer is: This refers to the case where, prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one relies on the dhyāna of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) to give rise to the roots of goodness such as "warmth" (*uṣmagata*).
Based on this, one enters the concentration of the formless realm (*ārūpyasamādhi*) with a mind seeking the path of seeing.
In this manner, progressing through the three emptinesses and giving rise to this practice is called the faculty of "the unknown that is to be known" (ājñātāvyajñāsyāmīndriya).
It does not mean that the three emptinesses themselves can enter the fundamental path of seeing (darśanamārga) and thus be called the faculty of "the unknown."
Question:
If that is so, then this person also relies upon the perception of non-existence to give rise to this contemplative practice.

In that case, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) should exist in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana). Why is it not mentioned?
Answer:

Because the three lower stages of the formless realm possess the remaining two untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), it is said that they possess "the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'" (*ājñātāvy-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).

As for the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), although the latter two untainted faculties are present there, the masters of the treatises do not say that this [faculty] exists.
Furthermore, because the mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is obscure and dull,
it cannot give rise to this practice as it can in the lower stages;
therefore, it is not said that the first untainted faculty exists there.
Question:
While the first untainted faculty (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) universally includes the nine tainted faculties of the preceding path of preparation (prayoga-mārga),

is it also permitted that, within the stage of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), it universally includes the nine faculties of the tainted path of preparation as the faculty of one who has already known (ājñendriya)?
The same applies to the question regarding the establishment of "one who possesses knowledge" (*ājñātāvī*) on the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
The commentary states:
The *Abhidharma-śāstra* says:
From the sixteenth moment of the path of seeing onwards,
throughout all stages of the path of training up until the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*),
the aforementioned ten faculties constitute the essence of the faculty of "I have known" (*ājñendriya*).
Therefore, it is known that the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātendriya*) is generally understood as being associated with the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation;
thus, the faculty of "already known" encompasses both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

Furthermore, the wisdoms of the three types—contaminated and otherwise—of those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of the two vehicles are also established as the faculty of "one who has fully known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
According to the Abhidharma, what is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
It is answered: the wholesome, afflicted, and neutral dharmas within the bodies of ordinary worldlings who have not yet sought liberation;
and the afflicted and neutral dharmas within the bodies of learners.

Within the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas as well as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas; these, along with that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*), are known to exist within the body of one beyond training.

Thus, it should be understood that the three types of wisdom associated with outflows (*sāsrava-prajñā*), innate goodness (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*), and so forth, are designated as the faculty of "one who has fully known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) within the body of one beyond training.
Master Ji said:
"The 'sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception' (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) is eightfold when categorized according to the path for abandoning afflictions;
however, if one includes [states such as] the meditative excursions (vihāra), it comprises eleven."
However, because the eleven factors of the sphere of infinite space are established as being identical to those in the *Abhidharma*,
and because all roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) are termed the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*),
these eleven factors contradict the preceding [definition].
This is based on the remote preparatory stage (*dūre-prayoga*).
As for the previous text’s reference to the fifteen moments of mind in the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), regarding these faculties:
one type is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), while another type pertains to both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted.
In one passage, it is stated that they are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) as well as unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*);
in another passage, it is stated that they are exclusively unbound.
In one passage, nine faculties (*indriya*) are given as their nature; in another passage, ten faculties are given as their nature.

There is a textual passage stating that the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) pervade even the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); therefore, the eleven faculties (*indriya*) of the sphere of infinite space mentioned in the preceding text are precisely these.
The remaining passages shall be reconciled later.
Now, consulting the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, fascicle seven, it says:
Those in the first three formless attainments who possess this faculty do so because they have acquired it through the subsequent cultivation following the path of vision (*darśanamārga*),
or because they were in the stage of the two vehicles and subsequently turned toward the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).
In order to realize the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*),
one also gives rise to the untainted realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) subsumed under the nine stages prior to the [Bodhisattva] grounds;
these are all likewise subsumed within this faculty.
Next, the various faculties (*indriya*) are distinguished according to whether they are with-outflows (*sāsrava*) or without-outflows (*anāsrava*).
This is explained generally as being present throughout the seven stages (*bhūmi*), both with and without outflows.
Regarding the faculties within the Stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), Jing says:
Regarding the categories of faculties in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), there is no untainted (*anāsrava*) state that severs afflictions;
however, within the single continuum of one body in that sphere, there can be untainted states of meditative observation belonging to its own level.
Thus, there are two types of statements.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "liberation from afflictions" and so forth:
this refers to the Arhat’s liberation of the faculties from the outflows (*āsrava*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which is termed "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).
This point is not denied.
However, when one enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) by means of a mind belonging to the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*),
then the seeds of the nine grades of the mind of revulsion establish that attainment of cessation.
The cessation attainment (nirodha-samāpatti) is untainted (anāsrava),
as stated in the sixty-two [treatises].
This indicates that the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) also possesses untainted meditative observation.
Tài explains these two meanings as follows: first,
he states that if one considers them according to their generic nature (*jāti-svabhāva*), liberation from non-perception (*asaṃjñi-vimokṣa*) is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).
If considered in relation to the body within the continuum of liberation, it should be said to be of two kinds.
One says:
if considered from the perspective of the category of contemplation according to principle, since non-perception (*asaṃjñā*) does not exist [there], it should be said to be with outflows (*sāsrava*).
If one speaks in terms of the subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) and its continuous application of principle-contemplation (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), it should be said that there are two kinds.
Master Ji (Jizang) alternatively states:
"The 'category' refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*) category of the specific stage (*bhūmi*) which is uninterrupted regarding the abandonment of afflictions."
Furthermore, that which is called "untainted" (*anāsrava*) by virtue of being liberated from afflictions refers to subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Tse cites two interpretations from the *Vyākhyā*.
One interpretation states that, regarding its essential nature and category, the non-perception (asaṃjñi) is exclusively contaminated (sāsrava);
however, regarding its subsequent attainment and continuity, the non-perception is both contaminated and uncontaminated (anāsrava).
Another interpretation states:
In terms of the fundamental subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the supramundane class,
"non-perception" (*asaṃjñin*) refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
In terms of the faculties within the continuum of the body that has exhausted the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), it refers to the faculty [of non-perception].
There are also those that are untainted (*anāsrava*).
The following clarifies the degree of attainment;
the text is divided into three parts.
First, the number of attainments is distinguished by way of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Within this,
the desire realm is first treated in general.
Next, they are distinguished according to the five destinies (*gati*),
and subsequently distinguished individually according to the continuity [of rebirth].
Regarding the initial statement, "all of the desire realm":
This is based on the fact that for many people, or even for a single person, it is possible throughout their entire life to possess twenty-two faculties (*indriya*).
Master Bei Jing says:
"According to the trend of the subsequent text..."
Generally speaking, that which arises in a continuous stream of manifest activity is termed "possession" (*samanvāgama*).
Next, regarding the passage beginning with "In the hells... and so forth," there are four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
First is the phrase concerning the simultaneous establishment of both the manifest and the seeds.
Eighth, regarding the two interpretations shared by Jing and Ji:
one states that the five faculties—eye and so forth—as well as life, mind, and suffering [are the basis].
This is discussed in terms of the six consciousnesses.
The second [position] states that one excludes suffering and adopts equanimity;
this is discussed in terms of the functioning of the eighth [consciousness].
Jingyun: The intention of the Tripiṭaka Master lies in the initial interpretation;
Śīlabhadra agrees with this.
Master Ji also stated that the former interpretation is superior:
although the feeling of equanimity coexists with the eighth consciousness and is constantly active, it is eclipsed by suffering.
It is not included because it is mentioned in fifty-one places [in other texts].
Furthermore, it is not included because it is established in relation to the six consciousnesses.
Now, let us examine the "Exclusively Suffering" realm as described in the fifth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Regarding the mental feeling of distress, there are two points of contention:
first, some say it should be named *daurmanasya* (sorrow);
second, others say it should be named only *duḥkha* (suffering).
This extensively refutes the previous master’s citation of this text as proof that the other three meditative absorptions each possess one of the feelings of pleasure, joy,
or equanimity. If the previous master claims that the passage merely speaks of "accommodation," [the response is as follows:]
In that case, one should not say that the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) is necessarily established,
because those six adventitious consciousnesses are sometimes absent.
Furthermore, how can it be said that [the faculties] are necessarily eight?
If it is argued that because the five consciousnesses do not continue in succession, sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is said to be the eighth [root],
then how could there be a faculty of sorrow during death, birth, or fainting?
Others maintain that the faculty of suffering (*duḥkha*) is the eighth.
This refutation applies equally here.
Furthermore, if one were to maintain that a single shape constitutes the eighth [element],
this is likewise unreasonable.
Because their form is not fixed;
since those evil karmas may manifest without a physical form,
yet because those [beings] cause the five sense-faculties to constantly experience suffering through that evil karma, they necessarily possess eyes and the other faculties.
Therefore, in this eighth dhyāna, there is the equanimity (upekṣā) of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses.
Just as the mind’s extreme joy in the Land of Ultimate Bliss is called "pleasure" (sukha),
so too the mind’s oppression in a place of extreme suffering is called "pain" (duḥkha).
Based on that [explanation], this equanimity is established as the eighth.
Second is the section on the certainty or uncertainty of seeds and manifestations;
excluding two types, there are three.
First, there are three untainted [factors].
Second, there are the three feelings.
Regarding this, Master Tai and others state that they take up joy (*prīti*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Bei states that one takes up sorrow, joy, and pleasure;
I now agree with Master Bei,
following the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
The remainder consists of the five faculties beginning with faith, as well as the male and female faculties and the faculty of suffering.
Jñānaprasthāna-bhāṣya (the *Ki*) states: "This phrase indicates that both the seeds and the manifest states are indeterminate."
This means that the manifestation of the two faculties of male and female is indeterminate as to their presence or absence;
if even the seeds were indeterminate,
it would be as stated in the text regarding those "without faculties."
The root-seeds are likewise impaired;
therefore, it is not the case that what is not currently active cannot constitute a seed.
This applies consistently to those included within the "possessing" (sopadhika) state, and the same holds for the five faculties of faith and so forth.
Just as one with wrong views damages and suppresses the seeds of goodness,
it is also called "non-formation of the seed.
This refers to the section on the three types of maturation within the text.

Therefore, it is not the case that because [the suffering] does not exist in its active manifestation (*samudācāra*), it cannot constitute a seed (*bīja*). It is certain that it exists within the state of being a seed;
for it has already been stated that within this state, even one who does not perceive suffering is subsumed under both the state of the seed and the state of active manifestation.
Now it is not so; for although the five faculties beginning with faith, as well as masculinity and femininity, may be impaired or suppressed,
their essential seeds still exist.
It is called "established as a seed" [only] when it is in a state of non-fainting; if one is in a state of fainting,
the faculty of suffering is interrupted.
Therefore, while the manifest is not established, the seeds are definitely existent.
Third, the phrase "the manifest is definitely non-existent while the seeds are indeterminate" refers to the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
Tai said:
"By this it is proven that all bodhisattvas from the first bhūmi upward do not receive the actual retribution-body of the hells,
because they have severed the karma and ignorance of the evil destinies."
Only the nirmāṇakāya goes [to the realm of rebirth].
As for Ajātaśatru’s understanding of parinirvāṇa,
it is because he was free from heavy obstructions.
The fact that untainted seeds possess the capacity for arising is thus established.
Paramārtha (Hushou) states:
"Because there exist innate untainted seeds."
The name "Matured" (paripakva) refers to the seeds that exist by nature (dharmatā-bīja), as explained in the second interpretation;
it refers to newly perfumed (navasaṃskṛta) seeds, as explained in the first interpretation.
Fourth is the proposition: "Presently non-existent, but definitely existent as seeds."
The third consists of sorrow, joy, and pleasure.
Master Jing and others say that it should instead be stated as "the other two."
That is to say, the two— joy and pleasure—
do not arise in the hells;
it is the seeds that reach maturation there.
Having carefully examined the Sanskrit original,
I shall not follow this explanation here.
As for the places where ghosts and animals experience suffering and pleasure in a mixed manner:
The latter three are also present and established;
"established" refers to sorrow, joy, and pleasure.
This is according to the preceding and following contexts.
I have not seen it stated anywhere that there is a place in hell where one experiences a mixture of suffering and pleasure.
Below, the distinctions are analyzed according to the continuity [of the mind],
resulting in six pairs of sixteen questions and answers.
First, the distinction between those with deficient faculties and those with complete faculties.
Regarding "those with deficient faculties, excluding five":
this means excluding the male and female faculties and the three untainted (anāsrava) faculties.
If one lacks male or female faculties, one necessarily lacks the three untainted faculties;
therefore, these are designated as the five types based on their non-arising in actual manifestation.
Second, the pair of "man" and "non-man."
Regarding the "five excluding the *pudgala*":
this also excludes the male, the female, and the three untainted (*anāsrava*) faculties.
Jing says:
There are also those who are *paṇḍaka* (eunuchs) who possess both male and female faculties;
they are termed *paṇḍaka* because these faculties do not arise constantly.
Here, however, the discussion is based on those who entirely lack both male and female faculties.
Therefore, it is said that five [faculties] are excluded.
Those with both sexual organs (ubhayavyañjana) and those without any sexual organs (avyañjana) cannot enter the state of an ārya,
because they do not possess the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya).
Tai says:
The former [definition] excludes the three types of untainted individuals and those with dual sexual organs because it concerns the non-arising of male and female;
the latter differs from the former because it concerns the absence of dual sexual organs after birth.
If one has already attained the state of a noble one (ārya) and subsequently loses the faculties,
or if one first loses the faculties and thus fails to enter the state of a noble one,
or if one has already attained the stages conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) and then loses the faculties— in all these cases, one may still enter the state of a noble one.
The meaning is the same as that of the Hīnayāna. Ji says:
"There is no further textual passage regarding this."
Therefore, it is known that those lacking the male or female faculties cannot enter the state of holiness (*ārya*).
Furthermore, if one were to act as in the Lesser Vehicle, there would be no hindrance;
for in that case, the male and female [faculties] do not exist in mutual dependence.
Those with both sexual organs lack the three untainted [paths].
Regarding the three types of abandonment— abandonment of roots of goodness and non-abandonment of roots of goodness—
the latter eight [paths] do not arise.
Regarding the four categories of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*):
ordinary beings do not give rise to the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
All noble ones are collectively termed "those who have seen the truth" (*dṛṣṭasatya*).
Therefore, there is "all. Regarding the five pairs of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*):
for those in training, excluding the one who possesses complete knowledge (*ājñātāvī*), there are twenty-one.
In the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), excluding the first two untainted [faculties] as well as sorrow,
there are nineteen.
These are categorized in relation to the six stages of the four paths and four fruits.
There are twenty [factors] for one entering the stream (srotāpatti-pratipannaka),
excluding the final two untainted [faculties].
There are twenty for the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala).
Excluding the first and last two untainted [paths],
the path of approach to the fruit of once-returner, the fruit itself, and the path of approach to non-returner may also each possess twenty [moments].
This applies if one transcends the paths of approach to the two intermediate fruits.
Excluding the last two untainted [moments].
If one is proceeding through the successive stages,
then the first and the last two untainted [moments] are excluded.
The fruit of non-returning consists of nineteen;
likewise, excluding the stage of the candidate for arhatship who is free from sorrow,
the fruit of arhatship also consists of nineteen.
Excluding the first two untainted [faculties] and sorrow.
Regarding the second point, which distinguishes eighteen [faculties] based on the form realm:
this excludes the male and female faculties, as well as sorrow and suffering.

Jingyun: Although the noble ones of the form realm do not possess the untainted faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," they nonetheless possess the tainted faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" associated with the form realm,
such as the stage of "heat" (ūṣmagata) and so forth.
Now, regarding those in the form realm who turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle and enter the state of a Sage:
they likewise first give rise to the Path of Seeing through the realization of the emptiness of phenomena (dharmas).
Therefore, they possess the untainted faculty of "not-yet-known" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya).
What fault is there in this?
Regarding the third point, the eleven [factors] distinguished by way of the formless realm are as follows:
the five beginning with faith, the mental faculty, life, equanimity, and the three untainted [faculties].
Question: Since those in the formless realm do not enter the path of seeing,
how can they possess the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya)?
Bei said:
"When an arhat of the formless realm gives rise to a mind associated with outflows,
they again contemplate the skillful means for entering the state of an arhat."
Thus, this refers to the meaning of observing one's original practice.
Regarding the statement that there are eleven principles for the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya),
it should not be like the meaning of an Arhat observing suffering, its origin, and so forth.
Tài says:

If an ordinary person attains the stage of "decisive distinction" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) but has not yet entered the state of a noble one (*ārya*) or attained detachment from desire to be born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
they will necessarily subsequently give rise to the stage of "penetrating distinction" (*prativedhabhāgīya*).
Thus, there are eleven [sections].
The eighth is the section on the acquisition and relinquishment of death and birth.
Within this, the acquisition and relinquishment of death and birth in the desire realm are explained first.
Next, the acquisition and relinquishment [of dharmas] in the higher realms is explained.
Generally speaking regarding the acquisition and relinquishment at death and birth,
each of the three realms possesses three types.
In total there are nine;
now we discuss the four seasons,
omitting the others for brevity.
Within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*),
the question is posed first and the answer follows.
Within the answer, the acquisition and relinquishment [of faculties] are first analyzed with reference to the contaminated (*sāsrava*) faculties.
The latter part clarifies the reason why the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) are not mentioned;
within the former part, the acquisition and relinquishment of the material faculties (*rūpīndriya*) are first distinguished,
followed by the acquisition and relinquishment of the immaterial faculties (*arūpīndriya*).
In the preceding section, the general principles were first set forth;
in the subsequent section, the specific cases of acquisition and relinquishment are distinguished.
Within this, the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) are first established by means of the deficiency and completeness [of the faculties].
Subsequently, the four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) are distinguished according to superiority and inferiority.
The preceding section clarified that those with deficient faculties and those with complete faculties both pertain to both the happy realms and the miserable realms;
the subsequent section clarifies their relative superiority and inferiority.
In that case, the faculties of those in the happy destinies are superior,
while the faculties of those in the miserable destinies are inferior.
If one dies in a happy destiny...
Being born in the evil destinies;
abandoning what is superior and obtaining what is inferior, and so forth.
Furthermore, it is explained as follows:
The former refers to the faculties of maturation (*vipākaja*),
while the latter refers to the faculties of nourishment (*aupacayika*).
Next, the acquisition and abandonment of the formless faculties will be analyzed.
First, distinguishing the maturation faculties— the mind faculty and the life faculty—
it is further analyzed that they are superior in the happy realms and inferior in the miserable realms.
Through clear comprehension, one attains equanimity.
As for the various faculties of sensation,
humans and devas possess superior wholesome joy and bliss.
In the miserable realms there is inferior sorrow and suffering;
one dies here and is born there.
Thus, there is the relinquishing of the inferior and the acquisition of the superior.
As appropriate,
the faculties of outflow are subsequently explained;
these refer to the five faculties, such as faith, which were previously cultivated through wholesome dharmas.
Even though they undergo further births,
there is only progress;
there is no relinquishing of what is superior to obtain what is inferior.
Except at the moment when one initiates the wrong means that sever the roots of goodness,
there is no relinquishing of the superior and acquiring of the inferior.
The following clarifies the reason why the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) are not mentioned.
It is contrary to birth and death;
since it lacks the sense of passing away from one life and being born into another— of acquisition and abandonment—
it is not mentioned here.
The preceding section has concluded the analysis of the acquisition and relinquishment of death and birth within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The following section clarifies the acquisition and relinquishment in the higher realms;
the text is divided into two parts.
First, the acquisition and relinquishment of the contaminated faculties (*sāsrava-indriya*) at death and birth are explained;
subsequently, the uncontaminated faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) are explained.
Within the former, the arising of form (*rūpa*) is first analyzed.
Regarding the second category of understanding:
what faculties are not relinquished in the higher stages?
Furthermore, what faculties cannot be attained in the higher stages?

The explanation is as follows:

generally, regarding abandonment, if one is in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and previously lacked the male or female faculties, or the eye, ear, and other such faculties, [one must first obtain them before abandoning the lower stage].
In this life, since there is nothing to be abandoned above,
it is said that one may abandon everything of the lower stages;
this applies to all faculties obtained upon reaching a higher stage.
That which exists can be attained;
that which does not exist cannot be attained.
For example, when one is born into the third dhyāna, joy cannot arise.
Because no pleasure can be obtained in the fourth dhyāna,
it is said that one may obtain all [faculties] upon being born in the higher realms;

The explanation has two parts:

From here on, the following verse concludes these eight sections.

Tai and Ji both state:
this is the correspondence between the teachings and the principles.

Each of the twenty-one faculties has its own respective referent.
Excluding the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).

The seven material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) are able to apprehend their respective objects only by relying on non-material factors such as visible form as their concomitants;

Master Ji said:
"The seven colors alone cannot function with respect to the meaning."
Only when accompanied by that which is non-material can [the mind] apprehend an object.

Now, considering what was explained previously—that among the eighteen elements, one element and a portion of another are capable of apprehension independently, without requiring assistance from companions—it is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Because the mental consciousness and its associated mental factors do not rely upon the five physical sense organs,
they are called "able to apprehend independently.
Why, then, does this passage state that other objects— whether they are material sense organs or non-material phenomena— serve as their auxiliary companions?
The commentary states:
"The words are general, but the meanings are distinct.
Furthermore, another interpretation says:
In the preceding passage, it was stated that [the mental consciousness] is "solitary" because its companions were defined in terms of sharing the same object; however,
in this present passage, companions are defined in terms of mutual dependence.
Therefore, all those [faculties] that function by means of the faculties (indriya) take both matter (rūpa) and non-matter as their companions.
Question:
Do the seven material faculties also depend upon the four objects (viṣaya) that support the faculties?
Why is it said that [the term] functions only in the sense of being a non-material auxiliary?
The explanation states:

Now, within the context of the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), this meaning is distinguished; it refers to those that support the faculties and their objects, yet are not themselves subsumed under the category of faculties.

Third, the section distinguishing the objects of apprehension (*grāhya-artha*) has twelve statements.
Regarding the statement that "the meaning of the male and female faculties, when associated with desire and greed, is subsumed under contact":
this means that because body-consciousness is associated with desire and greed,
the sense-object of contact (*spraṣṭavya*) constitutes its object.
The five faculties of sensation arise following the six faculties, such as the eye,
and take their respective objects as their domains.
Regarding the faculty of faith, its meaning is that which should be attained and that which should be abandoned.
One should acquire what is good and abandon what is evil.
Regarding the two kinds of diligence,
one should likewise acquire and abandon accordingly.
Regarding the meaning of the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*) as "stopping and contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*),
it takes the objects of focus for concentration and wisdom as its meaning;
alternatively, it may take concentration and wisdom themselves as its object.
Regarding the meaning of the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) as the true reality of what is known (*jñeya-tattva*),
Jing’s commentary states:
"While it takes the true reality of principle (*li-tattva*) as its object, it is also reckoned to take phenomena (*vastu*) as its object."
Now, to clarify that understanding the principle is called "knowing reality":
the meaning of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) up to the meaning of the five faculties— this refers to all the skillful means,
such as the generation of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), the seeds, and the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
All the roots of goodness that constitute the factors of the path are,
in their entirety, the essence of the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown";
they thus take as their objects the five faculties, beginning with faith.
The seventh chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi* also states this.
Jñānaprasthāna-bhāṣya (基) says:

"In this context, it is taught that the essence of the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) encompasses both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*)."
Thus, there are those bound to the three realms and those unbound;
and the fourfold gate of the material and the immaterial,
where "material" is the referent.
That is to say, with the exception of the seven material faculties and the life-faculty, fourteen faculties have both the material and the immaterial as their referent objects.
Question: How does the faculty of suffering take the material and the immaterial as its referent objects?
Master Jing and others explain that because sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is subsumed under suffering,
it is called the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
It universally takes the formless realm as its object.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the self-witnessing portion (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) of the faculty of suffering takes its own seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) as its object.
The explanation regarding the formless [realms] largely accords with the later exposition;
now, however, we shall follow the correct tenets of Dharmapāla’s *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
In the purely painful realms, there is suffering on the mental level (*manobhūmi*).
What prevents the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) from also taking the formless realm as its object?
It is simply because [suffering] is extremely subtle there.
It does not take the past or future as its object.
The life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is neither material nor immaterial;
"neither material nor immaterial" is its defining characteristic.
There is an interpretation that the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is neither matter nor mind;
thus, its meaning as a "root" consists in being neither matter nor mind.
Because it is a provisional designation based on states;

Jingyun: Because this life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is a conventional dharma,
its essence is neither material nor immaterial.
Nor does it take form or the formless as its object.
Fifth is the gate of the visible and the invisible:
all [of these] are not visible.
Jingyun: This corresponds to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) gate of the visible and the invisible.
Now, regarding the statement that there is "the visible":
The eye-faculty takes visible forms as its object;
because it is capable of seeing other things,
it is called "possessing visibility."
Furthermore, it is said that the sense-object (viṣaya) is "manifest" (sanidarśana).
Among all material forms (rūpa), the single category of the visual object (rūpaviṣaya) is the most coarse and manifest;
therefore, it is called "manifest."
It is also called "having manifestation.
Because the shadows of the objects of form (rūpa) manifest,
it is named "having manifestation."
The others are not so; they are not called "having manifestation.
Now, according to this principle, it is said that all [others] are non-visible.
This is said because the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*) are not themselves visible phenomena (*sanidarśana*).
Regarding the first point—that "possessing form" (*rūpin*) has "being visible" as its meaning:
since the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) possesses form, it takes "being visible to form-objects" (*rūpa-viṣaya*) as its meaning.
Furthermore, regarding those that are not of the nature of form (*rūpa*) but are partially so:

this refers to a portion of the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the five faculties associated with it such as faith (*śraddhā*), the five feeling-faculties (*vedanendriya*), the mind (*manas*), and among the three untainted (*anāsrava*) faculties, which also have a portion that takes visible form as its object.
Jizang further states:

The term "visible" (dṛśya) does not appear in the Sanskrit original;

That which is manifest can be demonstrated through signs,

The seventh is the gate of the tainted and the untainted.
The seven [elements of] form are tainted;
they grasp tainted objects.
The five mental factors beginning with faith— namely, faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom— as well as joy, equanimity,
and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya)— these ten are both contaminated and uncontaminated,
and they take both contaminated and uncontaminated objects.

because it gives rise to outflows and because it is associated with outflows.

Furthermore, because it serves as a guide to the untainted (anāsrava),
it is called "untainted.
The faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) exists within the five consciousnesses and takes only the five sense objects as its objective condition.

therefore, it is exclusively with outflows.
They universally take the four truths as their objects;
therefore, they have both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena as their spheres.
The latter two faculties, being exclusively uncontaminated, take only the uncontaminated as their objects.
The term "penetration" (prativedha) has the meaning of being both with-outflow (sāsrava) and without-outflow (anāsrava).
Regarding the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñātāvīndriya), it is distant from the fruit of the śramaṇa because it exists prior to the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
Recently, while examining the fifteen moments of mind in the Path of Seeing,
a question arose:
within the section on the three realms, the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is bound exclusively to the Desire Realm.
Why is it that within this [category] there is no untainted (anāsrava) [phenomenon]?
The explanation says:
the previous [classification] was based on intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Now, with respect to the continuity [of the stream],
there is no contradiction.
Eighth is the gate of the conditioned and the unconditioned.
