The remaining thirteen faculties take both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena as their objects, with the exception of the life-faculty.
There are nine gates concerning those with conflict and so forth.
Thirteenth Section on the Gates.
Jingyun said:
"If there are the faculty of form (*rūpendriya*) and the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) that exist in the past but are not [considered] 'past' in their meaning,"
This is based on a faculty existing in the present that takes the past as its object;
because it now flows into the past, it is called a "past faculty," taking the past as its referent.
When those possessing the material faculties (*rūpīndriya*) and the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) exist in the present, they do not take the past as their object,
because they have now entered the past;
therefore, one cannot say that the past has the past itself as its referent.
There is another interpretation: those sense-faculties (*indriya*) that can take the three time periods as their objects—
when "objects" (*artha*) are understood here as being past and present—
then they correspond to what was previously described as "a portion."
If the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) and so forth, while existing in the present, take as their object a future event that is about to arise—
such that the faculty-stream flows into the past and the objective-field-stream reaches the present—
then the past and the present are designated as "objects" (*artha*).
It should be understood that when that which has functioned as an object since the past arises in the present moment as a condition for a future event,
the sense-faculty flows toward the past while the object remains in the future, and thus [the cognition] does not arise.
Thus, the name "past" takes the future as its referent.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that this [present] exists in the present with the past as its referent:
it is also like a single moment of the mental faculty (manas) in the present taking objects of the past and future as its conditions.
When the sense bases do not arise with respect to past objects,
they are termed "past.
They take the past as their object and the future as their object.
Regarding the statement that "the present is the referent for those which are material and painful, as well as one portion previously mentioned":
this refers to the seven types of material suffering and the remaining [factors] such as the mind-faculty (*manas*).
As for their substance being in the present, one portion has the present as its referent.
Furthermore, regarding this portion [of the sense bases] that exists in the future and takes the past, future, and present as its objects: moreover,
a portion of the mental faculty (*manas*) and so forth, existing in the future,
will arise taking the three periods of time as its objects.
If the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) in the future do not have the future as their object, and the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is likewise so,
then even if the material sense-faculties were to arise in the present,
they would not take the future as their object.
Therefore, that which exists in the future does not take the future as its referent.
Ji says:
"As for the faculty of suffering and the seven material faculties, when they exist in the past, they do not take the past as their referent."
The Tripiṭaka masters state that these eight faculties, whether in the future or the past,
all have objects that exist in their respective times;
however, they speak of them as "non-existent" [in the present].
Furthermore, for example, when eight faculties are presently perceiving objects,
these faculties exist in the present; when the object enters the past,
and at the second moment the faculty subsequently perceives the next object and likewise enters the past, it is then termed "past."
It does not take the past as its object;
however, those present [factors] that share the same object enter together into the past,
and the past also takes the past as its object.
Regarding the current interpretation:
for instance, although the formless faculties exist in the present and currently take all three time periods as their objects,
it is explained according to the principles of the past and future that they each take the objects of the three time periods as their respective objects.
Because the eight [faculties] beginning with the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) take only the present as their object within the present,
they are metaphorically said to have "outflows" (āsrava) when they are past,
because their power is then weakened.
Because [the object] exists in the future and so forth,
it is not said that [consciousness] takes the present world as its object,
as explained previously.
Why is it that while the faculty (indriya) and the object (viṣaya) both exist in the present,
the faculty can take as its object one that has entered the past?
The commentary states:
Now, the present object-field (rūpāyatana) first enters the past;
the future eye-faculty (cakṣurindriya) enters the present;
and once the present eye-faculty has entered the past—
It cannot take the past as its object.
Furthermore, the sense-faculties and their corresponding forms that exist in the present both enter the past together;
thus, they cannot take past objects as their objects.
Eleventh is the classification by the three realms of existence.
Regarding the four factors bound to the desire realm that have the desire realm as their referent:

furthermore, because the image-aspect (nimitta-bhāga) arises from the seeing-aspect (darśana-bhāga) and belongs to the desire realm (kāmadhātu),

Regarding the second point— that the objects of desire and form are "desire" (*kāma*)—
the two faculties of nose and tongue are connected to both realms.

the same principle applies to the three [faculties]— eye, ear, and body— which are bound to both the desire and form realms (*kāmarūpadhātupratisaṃyukta*).
Regarding the statement that the two—those bound to the desire and form realms and those unbound—have as their meaning being bound to the three realms or being unbound:
this refers to joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*).
The same applies to the seven [factors] being bound to the three realms or being unbound.
That is to say, the five faculties beginning with faith and the faculty of equanimity of mind.
Regarding "having as its object all that is bound to the realm of form and that which is unbound":
this refers to the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya).

Jingyun: As stated previously, because one follows the wholesome dharma, the desire to depart [from suffering] constitutes the essence of the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) throughout all paths of skillful means;
this refers to the inclusion of both distant and proximate skillful means.
Now, having recently taken up and resolved upon the [topic of] conformity, it is said that [dharmas] are either bound to the realm of form (*rūpapratisaṃyukta*) or unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*).

Tài explains the two interpretations of the commentators:
one says that the four roots of goodness also extend to the formless realm;
the other says they are bound exclusively to the form realm.

Preface: Regarding the statement that the initial faculties exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), this is based on their remoteness from the wholesome factors of the desire and form realms (*kāmadhātu* and *rūpadhātu*).
[Next is] the section on the twelve faculties according to their three moral natures (*tridharmasvabhāva*).
Regarding the eight that are exclusively wholesome, their meaning consists of the three natures;
the five beginning with faith are the three untainted (anāsrava) states.
Regarding the five that pertain to all three natures, their meaning consists of the three natures.
Excluding sorrow, taking the four feelings and the mind:
that which is wholesome, unwholesome, or has the three natures as its object is the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Regarding the five indeterminate [faculties] having the indeterminate as their object:
these are the female, male, nose, tongue, and body faculties.
Regarding the two indeterminate [faculties] taking the three natures as their objects: [these are the eye and ear faculties].
Regarding "eye and ear," Master Ji says:
"This is based on the conventional designation of manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*)."
Thirteen are the gates of the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*).
Regarding those nine that pertain to the three trainings and take the three trainings as their meaning:
this refers to the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), and the seven—joy (*prīti*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—which likewise do not take [the three trainings] as their object.
This refers to the seven material faculties.
One type, which is neither of the three [other categories] nor has them as its object, is the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
This is because it is based on its intrinsic nature; therefore, it is said to be exclusively bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and has objects bound to the desire realm.
Now, because we are dealing with the three categories, all three types of conditions apply.
Since they are both induced by the contemplation of emptiness and the uncontaminated (anāsrava) contemplation, they are said to be "common.
Sorrow (daurmanasya), however, is not induced by the contemplation of emptiness, and thus it is not analogous.
Regarding the first [category], where both are to be cultivated and three are taken as the meaning:
this is the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Question:
Previously it was stated that the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is bound only to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*); now it is said to be pervasive.
Master Jing explains:

"The meaning of 'learner' (*śaikṣa*) is pervasive across both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*); however, only those wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma*) that involve further cultivation and progress are designated as 'learner'."
Master Ji says:

The meaning of the preceding passage is that because the faculty of "I do not know" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) is a portion of nine faculties, sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is bound exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The meaning of this present passage, however, follows the *Abhidharma*.
The first two untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) constitute its essence;
since they encompass ten faculties,
the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasya*) is included therein.
The second [category] conditions three.
The first two, being untainted (anāsrava), take the three types as their referent in the sense of being "in training" (śaikṣa).
Both [the first two], when known, take the three types as their referent in the sense of being "beyond training" (aśaikṣa).
Fourteen [factors] are abandoned through three gates.
Regarding those fourteen that are partially abandoned by vision and partially abandoned by cultivation:
this excludes the eight roots of goodness.
Among the remaining fourteen faculties, seven are material and the life-faculty;
those belonging to the miserable realms are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*),
while those belonging to the happy realms are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Question:

Jingshu, the Tripitaka Master, stated:

Beiyun says:
Following this same principle of correspondence,

According to the gate of ultimate truth,

"Beneficial inclusion" (saṃgraha-upakāra) has the meaning of growth and nourishment;

there are those that function based on a support but do not depend on an object,

Although it functions in dependence upon the body composed of the great elements,
because there is no consciousness coming to rely upon it,
it cannot apprehend objects and so forth.
Second, the various faculties are analyzed according to their singular or multiple bases.
That which is singular and has a single base refers to the *sabhāga* (functioning) faculties, which are based upon the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
The second support refers to the two supports of the homogeneous sense-faculties and the four great elements for their respective consciousnesses.
The third support is...

This is divided into four parts;
first, the differentiation of meanings.
Regarding the statement, "That which fully encompasses and maintains the meaning of all formations (saṃskāra) is therefore called a 'skandha'":
this comprehensively subsumes the three truths, and its scope of inclusion is exhaustive.
Therefore, it is said that they are "fully endowed" and so forth.
To clarify the meaning of repeated inclusion,
the term "layer upon layer" (重重) is employed.
Another interpretation is that the former term refers to the essence (the signified),
while the latter term refers to that which expresses it (the signifier).
Because its nature is such, it is established with this name;
the following should be understood accordingly.
It is that which constantly increases all karma and afflictions.
This is based on the fact that the aggregates of appropriation (upādāna-skandha) comprise only suffering, its origin, and the afflictions and karma;
for this reason, they are called "aggregates" (skandha).
They are so named because they constantly have something to do and because they quickly perish.
That which arises through volitional activity and quickly perishes is called an aggregate (*skandha*);
this applies to all three truths.
That which initiates all phenomena is called an element (*dhātu*), and so forth.
The eighteen elements (dhātu) draw forth all phenomena;
therefore they are called "elements.
As for the phrases "capable of producing" and "capable of expanding," [they refer to their causal efficacy].
It is called an *āyatana* (base) in the sense that it can produce and nourish the mind and mental factors.
Regarding the phrase "due to various conditions," etc.:
Because of the arising and ceasing through the gathering of the four conditions,
the "principle of origination" and so forth refers to the thorough knowledge of the principle of the equality of all phenomena.
Regarding "the mastery over activities such as seeing":
this refers to the mastery over the eye's act of seeing and so forth.
Second is the establishment of the analysis.
Thus, the six causes are sequentially assigned to the six types of skillfulness.
Jingzi’s commentary states:
"Cause" refers to the reason why.
First, the meaning of "accumulation" refers to this body;
one knows that the aggregates (*skandha*) are established as accumulations of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Second, one knows that the elements (*dhātu*) are established by way of the seeds of the eyes and so forth.
Third, one knows that the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) are the basis for the arising of the body of consciousness.

Fourth, one knows that the conditions upon which ignorance and the other factors depend are called the "expedient means of bondage," and thus they are established as dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Fifth, knowing that pleasure arising from the wholesome is called a superior means (*upāya*),
while pleasure arising from the unwholesome is called an inferior means;
this establishes the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna*).
Sixth, because one knows that each of those, such as the eye and so forth, has the sense of being a predominant factor for experience,
the faculties (indriya) are established.
The *Jī* (Jizang) says:
If it is that which is designated as a "person," then the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are the support for that person.
Third, the skillful exposition clarifies the departure from the six types of false attachments.
The commentary states:
First, knowing that the aggregates are impermanent and thereby abandoning the attachment to permanence;
second, grasping at primordial matter (*prakṛti*), self-nature (*svabhāva*), or Maheśvara as an uncaused or unequal cause.
Knowing that the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are the primary causes of all phenomena,
one abandons this attachment.
Third, non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) maintain that a self (*ātman*) sustains the sense faculties (*indriya*), perceives objects, and generates consciousness.
Through skill in the bases (*āyatana-kauśalya*), one knows that consciousness arises solely from the sense faculties and their objects,
thereby abandoning the false attachment to a self.
Fourth, those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) maintain that the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) over the preceding eighty thousand kalpas has a beginning.
After eighty thousand kalpas, there would be an end to birth and death;
however, through skill in dependent origination, one knows that birth and death have neither beginning nor end,
and thus eliminates false attachments.
Skillfulness regarding the five points of what is possible and what is impossible:
to clearly understand correct causes and effects is called purity;
to [understand] incorrect causes and effects is called impurity.
It can eliminate false attachments.
Sixth, through skillfulness regarding the faculties (*indriya*),
one understands that there are only the faculties that experience objects.
Thus, one is freed from all the false attachments of non-Buddhists who cling to a self that experiences desirable and undesirable objects.
Fourth is the discernment of the benefits,
as judged by the Tripiṭaka itself.
First, knowing there is no self dispels the notion of a unified whole; second, regarding phenomena that possess substantiality,
they appear to have an intrinsic nature and are perceived as true reality,
which is called "abiding in intrinsic nature."
Thus, one does not engage in slander;
thirdly, one is personally free from doubt,
and the True Dharma will abide for a long time.
Fourth, the penetration of dependent origination,
which is the nature of being without a creator;
fifth, the increase of wisdom through the thorough understanding of that which arises dependently.
Sixth, one should dwell correctly in mindfulness regarding the distinctions arising from wholesome and unwholesome conditions.
Seventh, because of practicing in accordance with the Dharma through the Dharma.
Eighth, because of realizing wholesome concentration by relying on correct dwelling in mindfulness.
Ninth, because one relies on wholesome concentration, noble wisdom shall arise.
Tenth, because one relies on noble wisdom, one abandons perversions and brings about the exhaustion of outflows.

third, through the six types of expertise, one personally eliminates doubt.

one is able to understand that Śakra, Brahmā, and others are not creators and lack substantial reality, and that the conception of a self as the cause [of existence] is termed the "Great Man" (puruṣa) and so forth.

Seventh, one abides with mindfulness regarding the wholesome, the unwholesome, and so forth,
by virtue of practicing in accordance with the Dharma.

Ninth, relying on meditative concentration,
noble wisdom shall arise.
